## Three Waves of Deep Learning in ER

1. **2017–2019 — Learned representations.** DeepER, DeepMatcher replace handcrafted similarity features with learned tuple/attribute representations (RNNs over word embeddings).
2. **2020–2022 — Pretrained LMs + learned blocking.** Ditto reframes matching as sequence-pair classification (up to ~+30% F1); AutoBlock / DeepBlocker make dense, label-free candidate generation practical.
3. **2022–2026 — LLMs.** From "train a matcher" to "prompt a matcher": few-shot GPT-3 beats fine-tuned Ditto on 4/7 datasets.

**Takeaway for direction choice:** pairwise *matcher* accuracy on small benchmarks is saturated. The frontier moved to **systems** questions — blocking, scale, cost.

---

## Wave 1a: DeepER (Ebraheem et al., PVLDB 2018)

- Compose each tuple into a distributed vector with uni-/bi-directional **LSTMs over word embeddings** (GloVe or task-tuned).
- Score tuple similarity on vectors — **no handcrafted features**.
- Blocking: **LSH over tuple vectors**, using *all* attributes instead of a few hand-picked blocking keys.
- Outperformed prior solutions on benchmark, biomedical, and multilingual datasets, with less labeled data.

---

## Wave 1b: DeepMatcher (Mudgal et al., SIGMOD 2018)

- Formalized neural EM as a **design space**: attribute embedding → summarization → alignment → aggregation → classification.
- Shipped as an **open-source Python package** inside the Magellan EM workflow (blocking → sampling → labeling → matching).
- Findings:
  - Deep models beat classical ML (RF/SVM over similarity features) on **textual and dirty** data.
  - But they need **large amounts of labeled data** and struggle on **structured/numeric** attributes.
  - Hybrid neural + classical is strongest.
- Side effect: standardized the **Magellan benchmark datasets** as the field's eval suite.

---

## Wave 2a: Ditto (Li et al., PVLDB 2020) — the strong baseline

- Cast EM as **sequence-pair classification**: serialize record as `COL attr VAL value …`, concatenate pair with `[SEP]`, fine-tune BERT/RoBERTa cross-encoder on `[CLS]`.
- Three optimizations: (1) **domain-knowledge injection** (highlight numbers, IDs, names); (2) **TF-IDF summarization** of long strings; (3) **label-preserving data augmentation**.
- Results:
  - Up to **~30% F1 over prior SOTA**; matches prior SOTA with **≤ ½ the labels**.
  - Real deployment (789K × 412K company matching): **96.5% F1**, where good blocking gave **3.8× end-to-end speedup**.
- Every later matcher paper compares against Ditto. "Beat Ditto on Abt-Buy" is a hard sell today.

---

## Benchmarks: why the classic suite is saturated

| Dataset | Domain | Labeled pairs |
|---|---|---|
| Amazon-Google | software | 11,460 |
| DBLP-ACM / DBLP-Scholar | citations | 12,363 / 28,707 |
| Walmart-Amazon | electronics | 10,242 |
| Abt-Buy | products | 9,575 |
| iTunes-Amazon | music | **539** |

- Newer, larger: **WDC Training** (26M offers, 20.7M positive pairs), **WDC Products** (multi-dimensional robustness), **Machamp** (heterogeneous schemas, CIKM 2021).
- The classic suite is **tiny and overused** — near-saturation and overfitting are real concerns.

---

## Wave 2b: Learned Blocking (2020–2024)

Blocking has opposite economics from matching: it needs very high **recall** (a missed match is unrecoverable) at extreme efficiency — and its output **prices the matcher**.

- **AutoBlock** (WSDM 2020): similarity-preserving representation learning + NN search; sub-quadratic, millions of records; no blocking-key engineering.
- **DeepBlocker** (PVLDB 2021): design space of 8 **self-supervised** deep blockers (no labels) + ANN search — the label-free dense-blocking recipe.
- **SC-Block** (ESWC 2024): supervised contrastive learning + FAISS/HNSW; **candidate sets ~50% smaller**, pipelines **1.5–4× faster**, no F1 loss; new WDC-Block benchmark (200B max pairs).
- **UniBlocker** (arXiv 2024): **universal** dense blocker — contrastive pretraining on generic tabular data, no per-domain tuning; **complementary to sparse blocking** (union improves recall).
- Consensus: dense buys semantic recall (synonyms, paraphrase); sparse is cheap and strong on surface overlap — **run both, union them**.

---

## Label Efficiency: attacking the annotation bottleneck

- **ZeroER** (SIGMOD 2020): zero labels — fit a GMM over similarity vectors to separate matches/unmatches; comparable to supervised on 5 benchmarks.
- **Transfer + active learning** (Kasai et al., ACL 2019): learn in high-resource setting, adapt with a few actively selected examples — **order of magnitude fewer labels**.
- **Sudowoodo** (ICDE 2023): contrastive self-supervised pretraining; **one shared embedder serves both the blocker (NN retrieval) and the matcher**.
- **DADER** (SIGMOD 2022): domain adaptation from labeled source ER datasets to unlabeled targets (six DA strategies).

---

## Wave 3a: Prompting LLMs for Matching (2022–2025)

- **Narayan et al. (PVLDB 2022):** GPT-3 **few-shot beat fully fine-tuned Ditto on 4/7 EM datasets** with a handful of demonstrations.
- **Peeters & Bizer (ADBIS 2023):** zero-shot ChatGPT reached **82.35% F1** where RoBERTa needed 2,000 training examples to match; similarity-based demo selection +7.85%.
- **MatchGPT (EDBT 2025):** systematic study — best LLMs rival fine-tuned PLMs with zero/few examples; key edge is **robustness to unseen entities** (fine-tuned PLMs memorize training entities); **no single best prompt** — must tune per model × dataset; GPT-4 can diagnose labeling errors.

---

## Wave 3b: Small Fine-tuned LLMs — the cost answer

- **AnyMatch** (arXiv 2024): zero-shot EM with a fine-tuned **GPT-2 (124M)** + smart data selection.
  - 2nd-highest overall F1 across 9 benchmarks vs 13 baselines.
  - Within **4.4%** of MatchGPT/GPT-4 at **3,899× lower** inference cost.
- **Jellyfish** (EMNLP 2024): instruction-tuned open models (7B–13B) on data-prep tasks incl. EM; competitive with GPT-3.5/4, runs on a single local GPU — the **self-hostable, privacy-preserving** matcher archetype.

---

## Beyond Pairwise Calls — and LLM Blocking

- **LLM-CER** (arXiv 2025): LLM performs **in-context clustering** over record sets (next-record-set creation, misclustering guardrail, transitivity-aware merge).
- **Retrieve–Match–Escalate** (2026): production cascade — per-record top-20 retrieval, cheap cross-encoder routes by confidence, only the ambiguous band escalates to an agentic VLM. Blocking/recall **explicitly bounds the funnel**.
- **Consensus on LLM blocking:** LLMs are prohibitively expensive for blocking (quadratic pairs × per-pair cost) — use them **selectively post-blocking**.
- **Shah et al. (Algorithms 2025):** blocking + fine-tuned LLaMA3/BERT improves **both runtime and F1** over LLM-only linkage. **Blocking remains critical in the LLM era.**

---

## Scalability: record-level vs pair-level blocking

- **Candidate generation prices the matcher.** With cross-encoder / LLM matchers, per-pair inference dominates — candidate-set size (and recall) is the scaling lever.
- **Record-level blocking:** per record, retrieve a bounded **top-k** (e.g., ANN k-NN over tuple embeddings). Volume O(n·k) — **predictable**, index-friendly, with a recall-vs-cost knob (**k**).
- **Pair-level blocking:** emit candidate **pairs** directly (e.g., all pairs co-occurring in key-based blocks). Volume is hard to bound and explodes on skewed blocks.
- **Why it matters:** expensive matchers need bounded, per-record candidate budgets — record-level maps cleanly onto ANN infrastructure; pair-level enumeration has no such knob.
- Metrics: Pairs Completeness (recall), Reduction Ratio, Pairs Quality (Papadakis et al., ACM CSUR 2020).

---

## Graph NNs: a smaller, specialized thread

Collective signals (transitivity, shared attributes/neighbors) that pairwise classifiers ignore:

- **HierGAT** (SIGMOD 2022): token → attribute → entity graph attention; attention surfaces discriminative tokens per decision.
- **GraLMatch** (EDBT 2025): **post-hoc** graph correction — build a graph from Ditto's predictions, remove false positives via transitivity constraints.
- **GraphER** (arXiv 2024): hybrid rule + learning — graph differential dependencies guide GNN representation learning; best on graph ER, competitive on relational.
- Theory is just beginning (GNN expressivity hierarchy for ER).

---

## Open Problems

1. **Blocking for the LLM era** — bounded per-record candidate sets for expensive matchers; learned sparse–dense hybrid blocking.
2. **Universal / zero-config blocking** — recall guarantees, automatic configuration, principled fusion of sparse and dense signals.
3. **Realistic large benchmarks** — WDC-Block is a start; missing: dirty multilingual, temporal, multimodal ER; evaluation on realistic post-blocking distributions.
4. **Collective ER at scale** — joint inference over clusters with guarantees, not post-hoc patches.
5. **Cost, calibration, trust** — per-pair LLM cost/throughput, prompt sensitivity, score calibration, privacy (hosted vs local), data contamination.
6. **Hard cases** — jargon-heavy domains, schema drift, identifier-heavy records where semantic models underperform symbolic ones.
7. **Fairness/bias** — blocking keys and embeddings vs protected attributes: essentially unstudied.

---

## Saturated vs Open

| Sub-area | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Supervised pairwise matching on Magellan-size benchmarks | **Saturated** — Ditto (2020) is a strong, simple ceiling |
| LLM prompting recipes for pairwise matching | **Crowded** — headline findings established (2023–2025) |
| Learned dense blocking (self-supervised + ANN) | **Open, high-impact** — recall–cost tradeoffs unsettled; universal blockers new; blocking *for* LLM matchers wide open |
| Scaling ER end-to-end | **Open** — cost models, cascades, large-scale evaluation just emerging |
| Collective / graph-structured ER | **Open** — young theory, young methods |
| Label-efficient ER | **Partially open** — active learning for *blocking config* underexplored |
| Trustworthy ER (calibration, fairness, privacy) | **Open** — barely studied |

---

## Recommendation: choose Scaling / Blocking

- A **scaling/blocking paper** has clearer headroom, a more direct industry audience, and **composes with** — rather than competes against — every matcher advance.
- The more expensive matchers get (LLMs), the more valuable blocking becomes: it prices the whole pipeline.
- If going the matcher route anyway, aim at an **unsolved axis**: OOD / unseen entities, identifier-heavy domains, multimodality, calibration — not another point of F1 on DBLP-ACM.
- Required: **method innovation, not benchmarking** — e.g., principled recall guarantees for learned blocking, cost-aware cascades, universal blockers with bounded per-record budgets.
